Francis Halzen, IceCube principal investigator and Hilldale and Gregory Breit Distinguished Professor at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, was announced yesterday as one of the prestigious international 2015 Balzan prizewinners. Luciano Maiani, former director of CERN and professor emeritus of theoretical physics at the Sapienza University of Rome read the citation for the assignment of the Prize for Astroparticle Physics including neutrino and gamma-ray observation to Francis Halzen. Maiani, who is a member of the prize committee, explained that the award recognizes Halzen’s “unparalleled accomplishments that have led to the construction of the large IceCube Neutrino Observatory in the south polar ice, a facility that has opened up a new window into the Universe through the study of cosmological high-energy neutrinos.” The Balzan Prize establishes four subject areas for each year’s awards, which for this year also included History of European Art, Economic History, and Oceanography. The prize committee decides on the winners from among the nominations entered by the world’s most important universities, research institutes and academies at the Foundation’s request. “Having been nominated by my colleagues and friends around the world means as much to me as the prize, if not more,” said Halzen after learning he was a 2015 Balzan prizewinner. His vision and scientific leadership have been fundamental for the IceCube Neutrino Observatory – a cubic kilometre of ice that is equipped with light sensors. Using IceCube, researchers can capture neutrinos from extremely energy-rich processes in the distant universe. Neutrinos are everywhere, but they do not make themselves known. They pass all the way through the Earth and through our bodies without us noticing. Very rarely, a single neutrino will interact with an atomic nucleus, which makes it possible for someone with the right equipment to discover them. Scientists have long known that the cosmos contains natural particle accelerators, which fire out particles with energies up to a million times more than can be achieved in laboratories on Earth. Much about these sources is mysterious: what are they, where are they, and what are the main processes inside them? Francis Halzen, IceCube principal investigator and Hilldale and Gregory Breit Distinguished Professor at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, was announced yesterday as one of the prestigious international 2015 Balzan prizewinners. Luciano Maiani, former director of CERN and professor emeritus of theoretical physics at the Sapienza University of Rome read the citation for the assignment of the Prize for Astroparticle Physics including neutrino and gamma-ray observation to Francis Halzen. Maiani, who is a member of the prize committee, explained that the award recognizes Halzen’s “unparalleled accomplishments that have led to the construction of the large IceCube Neutrino Observatory in the south polar ice, a facility that has opened up a new window into the Universe through the study of cosmological high-energy neutrinos.” The Balzan Prize establishes four subject areas for each year’s awards, which for this year also included History of European Art, Economic History, and Oceanography. The prize committee decides on the winners from among the nominations entered by the world’s most important universities, research institutes and academies at the Foundation’s request. “Having been nominated by my colleagues and friends around the world means as much to me as the prize, if not more,” said Halzen after learning he was a 2015 Balzan prizewinner. "IceCube: the discovery of cosmic neutrinos" (PDF). ... Francis Louis Halzen (born 23 March 1944) is a Belgian-American particle physicist and Nobel laureate. As of October 2026 he is the Vilas Research Professor and Gregory Breit Professor at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, and also the principal investigator of the IceCube Neutrino Observatory at the Amundsen–Scott South Pole Station in Antarctica, the world's largest neutrino detector. In 2026, Halzen was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics "for decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin." == Early life and ed

These were approved by Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez on October 6 and subsequently published in the Official State Gazette (BOE) on October 7. The first, Royal Decree-Law 29/2026, offers a comprehensive package of housing measures, while Royal Decree-Law 28/2026 focuses on the duration and renewal of standard residential lease agreements. Decrees Amidst Political Transition These decrees emerge after previous housing bills were rejected by parliament. The current scenario differs significantly as both the Congress of Deputies and the Senate are dissolved ahead of the general elections scheduled for November 29. Normally, the Congress of Deputies would vote on these decrees. However, with the dissolution of the legislative bodies on October 6, the Permanent Deputation of Congress now holds the authority to address these legislative texts until a new Congress is formed. Key Dates and Implementation Royal Decree-Law 29/2026 takes effect on October 8, 2026, just a day after its publication, with some provisions having their own timelines. This means that certain measures will start applying immediately without waiting for ratification by the Permanent Deputation. If the Permanent Deputation ratifies it, the decree remains in force; if not, it will be nullified instantly. Significant Housing Reforms Among the impactful changes for tenants is the reinstatement of an extraordinary lease extension of up to two years for select residential contracts. This allows tenants to request annual renewals, up to a total of two additional years, for contracts ending before December 31, 2028. Current Population Overview Total Population Estimates The 2024 Population and Housing Census by the Kosovo Agency of Statistics (ASK) reports the population of Mitrovica South municipality at 64,742, reflecting a decline of approximately 7,229 residents from the 2011 figure of 71,971.

[10] These ASK figures, while the most recent systematic data available, are contested in northern areas where actual residency may exceed reported numbers owing to incomplete registration and mobility; only 2,346 individuals were directly counted in North Mitrovica during the census process.

By 2000, international observers noted that North Mitrovica housed over 90% of the city's remaining Serb population, numbering around 10,000-12,000 individuals, forming a homogeneous enclave amid broader Albanian dominance in Kosovo.

[11] 2024 Census Challenges and Undercounting Claims The 2024 census in Kosovo, initiated by the Kosovo Agency of Statistics on April 5, encountered substantial obstacles in North Mitrovica due to a coordinated boycott by Serb political parties, including the Serbian List, which explicitly refused participation to avoid legitimizing Pristina's institutions.

[11] [6] The Kosovo Statistics Agency acknowledged that Serbs boycotted the process "to a considerable extent" following party directives, leading to incomplete data coverage in Serb-majority areas like North Mitrovica, Zveçan, Zubin Potok, and Leposaviq.

[11] [6] Undercounting allegations extended to practical consequences, including reduced municipal assembly seats and funding allocations in northern Kosovo, where North Mitrovica saw a reported population drop of 9,980 from 2011 estimates, exacerbating tensions over representation and resource distribution.

[30] Serb sources, while advocating for the boycott as a political statement, contended that the resulting data distorted demographic realities, potentially enabling arbitrary political manipulations in policy-making, though Kosovo officials maintained the figures reflected verifiable participation.

[34] Official and Everyday Usage In official contexts, Kosovo's Law on the Use of Languages (2006) mandates that Albanian and Serbian be employed equally in public administration, documentation, and signage throughout Mitrovica, with provisions for minority languages where applicable.

[43] [44] The 2024 Kosovo census, boycotted by most Serbs in northern municipalities including North Mitrovica, recorded only 7,920 residents there, yielding an undercount that the Kosovo Agency of Statistics acknowledged by pre-census estimates of about 53,000 Serbs nationwide.
South Mitrovica's population was 64,742 according to Kosovo's 2024 census, [1] with ethnic Albanians forming over 96% of residents based on 2011 census data adjusted for minimal minority returns.

[2] Overall municipal population is estimated around 90,000-100,000 when incorporating pre-2024 northern figures, with minorities like Bosniaks, Roma, Ashkali, and Turks present in smaller pockets amid ongoing emigration and declining birth rates characteristic of Kosovo's demographic trends.

This ethnic binary drives social and political dynamics, including parallel institutions and periodic violence, while source credibility varies: Kosovo Agency of Statistics data prioritizes registered participation but underrepresents Serb areas, whereas OSCE profiles incorporate field estimates to address boycott effects.

Historical Context Pre-1999 Ethnic Composition Prior to the Kosovo War in 1999, the municipality of Kosovska Mitrovica (encompassing areas now divided into North and South Mitrovica) featured an Albanian ethnic majority alongside a substantial Serb minority and smaller groups including Montenegrins, Bosniaks, Roma, and Turks.

[3] The 1991 Yugoslav census, however, faced significant challenges due to a widespread boycott by the Albanian population protesting Serb-dominated governance under Slobodan Milošević's administration, leading to estimated rather than directly enumerated figures for Albanians based on projected growth rates (assumed at 30.5% over the decade).

[5] [3] No official census occurred between 1991 and 1999, but anecdotal reports and vital statistics suggest continued Albanian growth and Serb outflows, setting the stage for post-war divisions, though exact pre-war urban breakdowns within Mitrovica city remain unavailable due to integrated neighborhoods.
[5] Post-1999 Displacement and Migration The Kosovo War culminated in NATO's 1999 intervention, leading to the withdrawal of Yugoslav forces and the establishment of UNMIK administration.
UNHCR documented over 200,000 Serbs displaced from Kosovo overall by mid-1999, with Mitrovica's southern areas seeing near-total Serb exodus as Albanian militants targeted Serb enclaves.
Violence peaked in June-July 1999, including the June 28 Zvečan mine attack killing 11 Kosovo Serbs and subsequent riots displacing hundreds more from southern Mitrovica.

KFOR forces struggled to maintain order, reporting over 1,000 incidents of ethnic violence in the region by year's end, accelerating Serb migration to northern Mitrovica or across the administrative boundary to Serbia proper.
Serbian government data claims 8,000-10,000 Serbs left Mitrovica municipality alone post-1999, though Kosovo Albanian authorities contested these figures as inflated.

This natural boundary has reinforced ethnic segregation since the 1999 Kosovo War, when mass displacements concentrated Serbs north of the river and Albanians south, culminating in the administrative division of the city into two municipalities in 2013 amid the North Kosovo crisis.

[14] These variations underscore methodological biases: Kosovo's census excludes non-participants in the north, while Serb-aligned estimates may incorporate cross-border commuters from Serbia proper, complicating verifiable enumeration.
South Mitrovica, by contrast, integrates into Kosovo's Albanian-majority framework, encompassing denser urban and industrial zones.

This division perpetuates low inter-communal mobility, with most residents rarely crossing the river, exacerbating socioeconomic disparities—northern infrastructure lags due to disputed funding, while the south benefits from EU and Kosovo investments.

The 2011 Kosovo census, administered by the Kosovo Agency of Statistics, recorded a total population of 71,909, with ethnic Albanians constituting 96.6% (69,497 individuals), reflecting near-homogeneity in the district following post-1999 demographic shifts.

[15] Recent estimates suggest a slight population decline due to emigration trends common across Kosovo, with South Mitrovica's residents numbering around 64,000 as of 2024, maintaining the Albanian proportion at over 96%.

[14] This composition stems from historical migrations, where the Serb presence in the south eroded sharply after 1999 amid interethnic violence and return barriers, leaving Albanian returnees and locals as the primary demographic.

International observers, including the OSCE, have noted the de facto ethnic segregation along the river divide, with South Mitrovica functioning as an Albanian enclave integrated into Kosovo's administrative framework.

[15] [16] Serb Majority in North Mitrovica North Mitrovica, the northern section of the divided city, maintains a Serb ethnic majority as a direct result of post-1999 Kosovo War displacements, where ethnic Serbs concentrated in the area north of the Ibar River to escape violence and maintain community cohesion.
Following the NATO intervention in June 1999, an estimated 80,000-100,000 Serbs fled Kosovo-wide, with many from southern Mitrovica relocating northward, solidifying the demographic shift.
Reports from 2023 indicate minimal Albanian presence in the north, estimated at under 500 individuals, often in isolated pockets or as returnees under international protection programs.

Minority Groups (Bosniaks, Roma, Turks, etc.) In Mitrovica, minority groups beyond the Albanian and Serb majorities include Bosniaks, Turks, Roma, Ashkali, Egyptians, and Gorani, who collectively represent a small fraction of the population and have faced significant displacement following the 1998-1999 Kosovo conflict.
They maintain community institutions, including schools, and have limited representation in local police forces (e.g., 1 in the municipal station).

[11] This led to official results covering only about 93% of Kosovo's territory, with final national figures at 1,739,825 inhabitants, underrepresenting Serb populations.

Fields typecode and registration are empty when the aircraft is not present in the database. Description of the dataset One file per month is provided as a csv file with the following features: callsign : the identifier of the flight displayed on ATC screens (usually the first three letters are reserved for an airline: AFR for Air France, DLH for Lufthansa, etc.) number : the commercial number of the flight, when available (the matching with the callsign comes from public open API) aircraft_uid : a unique anonymised identifier for aircraft; typecode : the aircraft model type (when available); origin : a four letter code for the origin airport of the flight (when available); destination : a four letter code for the destination airport of the flight (when available); firstseen : the UTC timestamp of the first message received by the OpenSky Network; lastseen : the UTC timestamp of the last message received by the OpenSky Network; day : the UTC day of the last message received by the OpenSky Network.
